items.title: Mercato cinese: le elettriche doppiano le termiche e fanno bingo nella Top Ten
items.description:
Il mercato automobilistico cinese parla sempre più… elettrico. Ad agosto le vendite al dettaglio di auto con motore…
L'articolo Mercato ci
items.body:
Il mercato automobilistico cinese parla sempre più… elettrico. Ad agosto le vendite al dettaglio di auto con motore termico sono crollate del 40% su base annua, mentre le BEV fanno registrare l’ennesima crescita. Ancora più netto il segnale della classifica dei modelli: nove delle prime dieci auto più vendute in Cina sono 100% elettriche.

Secondo i dati della China Passenger Car Association (CPCA), ad agosto in Cina sono state vendute 1,54 milioni di autovetture.

I veicoli NEV (New Electric Vehicles) – che comprendono elettriche pure, plug-in e, in misura marginale, veicoli a idrogeno – hanno raggiunto 1,005 milioni di unità, pari al 65,2% delle vendite. Le auto con motore endotermico si sono invece fermate a circa 536.000 unità, quindi quasi la metà delle NEV e in calo enorme rispetto ad un anno fa (ad agosto 2025 ne erano state vendute ben 894.000).
La loro quota di mercato in Cina ad oggi è scesa al 34,8%.

Il ridimensionamento non riguarda certo soltanto la classifica di agosto. Nel periodo gennaio-agosto le vendite delle NEV sono cresciute esponenzialmente raggiungendo le 6,7 milioni di unità, contro le circa 5 delle vetture termiche.

La dinamica più interessante riguarda la composizione delle vendite elettrificate, sospinte quasi del tutto dalle elettriche pure. Anche ad agosto, infatti, le BEV hanno fatto la voce grossa (+1,7% su base annua e + 7,9% rispetto a luglio), di fatto più che doppiando le vendite delle “sorelle” ibride plug-in (PHEV), che, al contrario, sono in calo per l’ottavo mese consecutivo.

Le auto elettrificate continuano inoltre ad avere una bella valvola di sfogo nelle esportazioni, salite del 154,7% su base annua.

La Cina avvia una graduale riduzione degli incentivi sulle EV

La fotografia diventa ancora più significativa osservando la Top-10 dei singoli modelli. Ad agosto, nove delle dieci auto più vendute in Cina sono state elettriche a batteria. L’unica eccezione è la Fang Cheng Bao Ti7 di BYD, ibrida PHEV comunque disponibile anche in versione BEV.

In cima alla classifica si è piazzata la Geely EX2 (39.651 unità), seguita dalla Leapmotor A10 e dalla Tesla Model Y. Per comprendere la varietà del mercato elettrico cinese odierno, Tesla è stato l’unico costruttore con due modelli nella Top-10 (Model 3 al 6° posto).

Importante rimarcare come in questa graduatoria non ci sia nessuna auto esclusivamente termica. La prima è la Toyota Corolla, al 13° posto con 14.675 unità. È la seconda volta quest’anno che le vetture a benzina rimangono fuori dalle prime dieci posizioni di una classifica mensile.

Questi numeri rappresentano un indicatore importante, soprattutto perché la trasformazione non sembra limitarsi alla semplice crescita delle auto “new energy”. All’interno di questo segmento è chiaro come siano le BEV a mostrare una maggiore capacità di tenuta, mentre le PHEV stanno arretrando.

Per l’industria europea il messaggio non è che la Cina abbia già trovato una formula universale per la transizione. Il mercato cinese non è infatti automaticamente replicabile in Europa, ma questi numeri pongono una domanda difficile da evitare. Quanto velocemente potrà cambiare anche il mercato continentale quando le elettriche diventeranno competitive non solo sul piano ambientale, ma anche su prezzo, prodotto e costi di utilizzo?

items.title: Transport & Environment: le ibride plug-in inquinano ogni anno di più
items.description:
Le ibride plug-in europee emettono molta più CO₂ nella realtà quotidiana di quanto non dicano i valori ufficiali…
L'articolo Transport & En
items.body:
renzo

il 10 Settembre 2026	L’attuale impianto normativo in materia di fringe benefit per i veicoli aziendali presenta un’evidente distorsione. La previsione di un’aliquota agevolata del 20% per le vetture ibride plug-in (PHEV) — a fronte del 10% riservato alle elettriche pure (BEV) — spinge gli utenti a privilegiare la tecnologia ibrida. Nella prassi quotidiana, tuttavia, questi veicoli vengono impiegati quasi esclusivamente con alimentazione a benzina, trascinando il peso supplementare del pacco batterie e del motore elettrico con un conseguente peggioramento dell’efficienza energetica.Per disincentivare un utilizzo difforme dalle finalità ecologiche della norma, l’aliquota per le PHEV andrebbe incrementata a una soglia vicina al 40%, allineandola maggiormente alle motorizzazioni a più alto impatto. Un adeguamento di questo tipo favorirebbe il definitivo superamento delle soluzioni ibride, spesso adottate come mero compromesso fiscale, a vantaggio di una reale transizione verso l’elettrico puro.
Rispondi

Massimo Degli Esposti

il 10 Settembre 2026	Per quel che conta, la pensiamo esattamente così anche noi: è assurdo investire in incentivi per auto che, nei fatti, inquinano come le termiche. Tra l’altro le plug-in sono un fenomeno principalmente italiano. In Europa ne circolano poco più di un milione, contro 7,6 milioni di elettriche pure.
Rispondi
		Edwin Abbott

il 9 Settembre 2026	Dopo il Diesel-gate, lo hybrid-gate!?Ci vogliono proprio morti a tutti i costi.
Rispondi
		Ivan

il 10 Settembre 2026	Se la gente è scema e compra una plugin senza ricaricarla la non è colpa della tipologia di auto
Rispondi
		Bob

il 10 Settembre 2026	Hai ragione, ma visto che alcune persone non agiranno mai in modo socialmente/economicamente/ecc…  sostenibile. Compito della politica dovrebbe essere quello di regolamentare in modo che siano costretti a farlo per motivi oggettivi.
Le soluzioni sono poche. La prima è far pagare i carburanti in modo da scoraggiarne l’uso. La seconda e forse più semplice; ovvero è regolamentare in modo che le auto PHEV/REEV/ecc… abbiano serbatoi di carburante non superiori ai 10 litri (10 litri a 20 km/lt fanno circa 200 km percorribili) tra riserva e utilizzabile. In pratica, rendi l’andare dal benzinaio più scomodo che ricaricare a casa una sera sì e una sera no. Tra parentesi si potrebbe obbligare un retrofit a tutte le auto per montare serbatoi da 10 lt  e tra nuove e vecchie PHEV si risolverebbe il problema alla radice.
Rispondi
		Bob

il 10 Settembre 2026	Dimenticavo, c’è anche una terza possibilità. Obbligare, a cadenza annuale, i proprietari di PHEV a presentarsi in un centro di revisione che hanno l’opportunità di leggere i dati delle emissioni di CO2 e far pagare una carbon tax per il delta in più di emissioni fatte rispetto al dichiarato WLTP. Tanto i dati della centralina non possono essere omessi.

The post Clima, agosto 2026 il più caldo della storia ap
items.body: In evidenza WWF Italia: 60 anni per la natura In evidenza Il Panda Siamo Noi In evidenza L'orso bruno marsicano In evidenza Adotta una specie WWF: “I dati diffusi da Copernicus dovrebbero mobilitare i governi del Pianeta” Agosto mai così caldo da quando si misurano le temperature medie terrestri. Dopo nove mesi, la temperatura globale sale oltre la soglia di 1,5 gradi rispetto all’epoca preindustriale. La temperatura media globale dell’aria superficiale ha raggiunto 16,96 gradi centigradi, 0,85 gradi sopra la media 1991-2020 e 1,65 gradi sopra quella stimata per il periodo preindustriale 1850-1900. A rilevarlo è il Copernicus Climate Change Service (C3S), implementato dal Centro europeo per le previsioni meteorologiche a medio termine (ECMWF), nel nuovo bollettino climatico mensile. Agosto 2026 è stato il primo mese a superare nuovamente la temperatura media globale di 1,5 gradi centigradi dal novembre 2025. In Europa, gran parte delle regioni occidentali e meridionali hanno registrato temperature sopra la media, con un +3°C di Francia e Italia.  Il dato non riguarda soltanto l’atmosfera. Nell’agosto 2026 la temperatura superficiale media degli oceani, tra 60 gradi Sud e 60 gradi Nord, ha superato i 21°C: è il valore più alto mai osservato per agosto e gli scienziati rilevano che le temperature record per mari e oceani si sono protratte per oltre tre mesi. La crisi climatica sta portando il Pianeta e suoi abitanti verso territori nuovi e potenzialmente molto pericolosi. Già oggi sta producendo fenomeni estremi nell’atmosfera e negli oceani, con impatti sempre più evidenti nelle comunità, nelle economie e negli ecosistemi di tutto il mondo. Questi dati dovrebbero spingere i Governi di tutto il mondo ad agire insieme e in fretta, dovrebbe indurre tutti a mettere la crisi climatica in cima alle priorità. WWF Italia In Europa caldo e siccità, allarme fiumi in secca In Europa il caldo è stato accompagnato da una siccità molto estesa, dalla Gran Bretagna all’Europa Meridionale . Ad agosto condizioni più secche della media hanno interessato alcune aree dell’Europa occidentale e vaste regioni dell’Europa centrale e orientale. I suoli superficiali hanno raggiunto livelli di umidità eccezionalmente bassi nelle zone colpite dalla siccità, mentre aridità e incendi hanno interessato diverse regioni del continente. Particolarmente significativo il segnale proveniente dai maggiori fiumi europei: Danubio e Reno hanno registrato portate eccezionalmente basse. come anche Vistola, Rodano, Senna. In Italia Po e Sesia sono ai minimi storici. Il questionario “Senti già la crisi climatica?” Il WWF Italia invita i cittadini a far emergere il peso dell’impatto dei fenomeni climatici sulla propria vita. Per aiutarli, l’associazione ha promosso, con il sostegno del Movimento Laudato Si’ e altre realtà civiche, un’indagine partecipata per analizzare l’impatto concreto della crisi climatica sulla vita quotidiana della popolazione. Senti già la crisi climatica? Partecipa alla nostra indagine per analizzare l'impatto concreto della crisi climatica nella vita delle persone Partecipa 5 Giugno 2026 Giornata mondiale dell'ambiente, parte l'inchiesta WWF Il WWF lancia un questionario per capire come la crisi climatica sta trasformando la nostra quotidianità 10 Luglio 2026 Clima, un giugno da record L'ondata di calore ha superato i record mensili e storici in vari Paesi europei, provocando gravi ripercussioni sulla salute 1 Luglio 2026 7 italiani su 10 sostengono il principio "chi inquina paga" Nuovo sondaggio europeo: la maggioranza degli intervistati non approverebbe un ridimensionamento del sistema europeo per limitare le emissioni di CO2 nei settori industriali

Il superamento di 1,5 °C potrebbe verificarsi già nei prossimi anni

Particolare della copertina del rapporto UNEP
                                            
                
                
                    Il nuovo rapporto del Programma delle Nazioni Unite per l’Ambiente UNEP “Limiting Overshoot: Navigating exceedance of 1.5 °C and pathways towards return” analizza gli scenari che si aprono con il probabile superamento della soglia di 1,5 °C di riscaldamento globale e individua le condizioni necessarie per limitare la durata e l’entità di questo superamento.
Secondo il rapporto, il riscaldamento causato dalle attività umane si sta avvicinando a 1,4 °C rispetto ai livelli preindustriali e il superamento di 1,5 °C potrebbe verificarsi già nei prossimi anni. Anche nello scenario più ottimistico, basato sull’attuazione degli attuali impegni dei governi, il riscaldamento globale potrebbe raggiungere un picco di circa 1,8 °C.
L’UNEP sottolinea che il superamento di 1,5 °C, definito overshoot, non deve essere considerato come un singolo momento, ma come un percorso articolato in una fase di superamento, un picco, una successiva diminuzione delle temperature e, infine, una stabilizzazione. Quanto più basso e breve sarà il periodo di overshoot, tanto minori saranno i rischi e gli impatti associati.
Il rapporto evidenzia che non esistono scenari privi di conseguenze oltre 1,5 °C. L’aumento delle temperature comporta rischi crescenti per gli ecosistemi, le risorse idriche e alimentari, la salute, le città e le infrastrutture, oltre a possibili cambiamenti irreversibili nei sistemi climatici e naturali.
Per limitare il picco di riscaldamento e creare le condizioni per un successivo ritorno al di sotto di 1,5 °C, l’UNEP indica come indispensabile una rapida e sostenuta riduzione delle emissioni di gas serra, compresi metano e altri inquinanti climatici di breve durata. Mitigazione e adattamento devono procedere contemporaneamente: mentre la prima contribuisce a limitare l’entità del cambiamento climatico, il secondo deve preparare società, territori ed ecosistemi a condizioni climatiche sempre più difficili.
Il rapporto considera inoltre necessario il ricorso alla rimozione dell’anidride carbonica dall’atmosfera negli scenari che prevedono un ritorno sotto 1,5 °C. Queste tecnologie, tuttavia, non possono sostituire la riduzione delle emissioni alla fonte e presentano ancora rilevanti limiti tecnici, economici e ambientali.
L’UNEP evidenzia infine che un eventuale ritorno delle temperature al di sotto di 1,5 °C non riporterebbe il sistema climatico alle condizioni precedenti: alcune conseguenze del riscaldamento saranno irreversibili. Per questo motivo, le decisioni adottate nel presente restano determinanti per contenere il picco di temperatura, ridurre la durata dell’overshoot e limitare i rischi futuri.
Per approfondire: UNEP, Limiting Overshoot: Navigating exceedance of 1.5°C and pathways towards return, 2026.

items.title: A strengthening yet less extreme Atlantic–European jet during winter
items.body:
Download PDF

Article
    
        
            Open access

Published: 10 September 2026

A strengthening yet less extreme Atlantic–European jet during winter
                        Stefan Brönnimann 
            ORCID: orcid.org/0000-0001-9502-79911,2, Yuri Brugnara1,2 & Patrick Kallabis1,2

Nature Geoscience
                             (2026) Cite this article
                        
                        
                            
                                
    
        
            
            
                
            Save article
            
        
        
            
                View saved research

AbstractThe Atlantic–European jet stream is a key driver of weather extremes in Europe, yet its recent variability and trends remain poorly understood. Here we investigate daily changes in jet strength, tilt and latitudinal extent from 1725 to 2100 using pressure data from four European stations alongside climate model simulations. These indices explain about 40% of day-to-day temperature variability in Western Europe year-round. Weather extremes—including heat waves, cold spells, heavy precipitation and windstorms—are closely linked to the jet stream, and the indices also capture signals of sudden stratospheric warmings and major solar storms. Since the pre-industrial period, the jet has strengthened by 0.13 standard deviations and shifted poleward during the cold season. Future projections indicate continued strengthening in winter, while extremes in the indices become less frequent, suggesting a potential reduction in some types of weather extremes.

Explore related subjects
            Discover the latest articles and news in related subjects.
            
                
                    
                        
                            Atmospheric dynamics
                    
                
                    
                        
                            Attribution
                    
                
                    
                        
                            Climate change
                    
                
                    
                        
                            Projection and prediction

MainThe jet stream over the Atlantic–European region strongly affects the weather in Western and Central Europe1. Temperature extremes such as cold-air outbreaks or heat waves are often related to specific configurations of the jet, while other configurations can bring heavy precipitation events2,3. Trends in the jet are not well understood. The jet in the North Atlantic has strengthened over the period 1951–2020, but this trend is not reproduced by climate models4,5. In fact, the observed strengthening is greater than in any one of the Coupled Model Intercomparison Project 6 (CMIP6) simulations6,7 and seems to be in large part independent of natural variability8. The suggested physical mechanisms behind the trend include, among others, diabatic heating9. A global northward shift of the jet is becoming apparent in observations over the satellite era, but this trend is mostly driven by the Asian and North Pacific sectors10.CMIP6 models project a strengthening and narrowing of the North Atlantic jet in winter11 as a result of the tug of war between the Arctic amplification at the surface and the warming in the tropical upper troposphere12. A weakened Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation can also cause a strengthening of the northern hemispheric jet in winter13.Given the large underestimation of the strengthening by CMIP6 models in the historical period, there is little confidence in the projected future trends14,15. In light of these results, it is crucial to analyse past changes in the jet stream variability. However, almost all studies on jet stream trends use three-dimensional data from atmospheric reanalyses such as ERA516 and therefore are limited to the past few decades, whereas studies based on climate proxies only cover the seasonal timescale and the results are sometimes contradicting14.Using a monthly, three-dimensional climate reconstruction17, we recently analysed monthly-to-seasonal jet stream variability back to 1421 by projecting 500-hPa geopotential height (GPH) anomaly fields onto three base patterns18 (north–south gradient, east–west gradient and midlatitude ridge decreasing north- and southward; Extended Data Fig. 1). However, the eddy-driven jet is a transient phenomenon and studying its links to extreme weather such as storms, heavy precipitation and cold or warm extremes requires daily data, which have so far only been available for the period since around 1940. Here, we present and analyse multicentury daily jet reconstructions and compare them with data on weather extremes and with jet indices in long coupled and uncoupled climate model simulations. This allows addressing the driving forces of trends in the mean and in extremes of the jet indices.Constructing daily indicesDaily air pressure series reaching approximately 300 years back are available from London19, Paris20, De Bilt19, Padova21 and Uppsala22. The latter two measure the north–south pressure gradient, while London captures pressure variations in Western Europe (Fig. 1, top left, yellow dots). To capture the west–east gradient and the ridge pattern, an additional series further east is needed. In Berlin, pressure measurements started in 1721, but only data since 1876 have been available so far. We digitized and processed the earlier part of the record (Supplementary Table 1), generating a long, complete, homogeneous daily pressure record (Methods).Fig. 1: Weather patterns associated with jet stream indices.Full size imageCorrelation coefficients between daily indices and 500-hPa zonal wind (shading, blue contours indicate the climatology) and GPH (grey contours) (first and second column), 2-m air temperature (shading) and sea-level pressure (contour) (third and fourth column) and precipitation (shading) and blocking frequency (contours) (fifth and sixth column) in the cold and warm season, respectively. The contour interval is 0.2 centred around zero, and negatives are dashed. All analyses are based on ERA5 deseasonalized data from 1940–2020 and use the Pearson correlation except precipitation (ECA&D, 1950–2020, nondeseasonalized, Spearman correlation). Yellow dots (top left) indicate the stations used for the indices; circles indicate correlations with daily temperature observations (1765–1864).On the basis of the four series, we formed three indices (strength, tilt and latitude; Extended Data Fig. 1) that are largely mutually independent (Methods). Calculating them within ERA5 and correlating with 500-hPa zonal wind (Fig. 1, left) shows a monopole on the jet axis for strength, a quadrupole around the jet axis for tilt and a dipole north and south of the jet axis for jet latitude. We also analysed a dataset of position and speed of the polar front jet (PFJ) at 315 K and of the subtropical jet at 350 K covering 1941–202423. We composited jet positions for indices below the 2nd or above the 98th percentile per season (Extended Data Fig. 2). For strong index cases, the PFJ is zonal, whereas for weak cases, it is diverted to the Mediterranean in the cold season (November–April) but to the North in the warm season (May–September). A positive tilt index is associated with a northwest–southeast tilt of the PFJ. The latitude index is associated with a strong latitudinal shift in the PFJ. Hence, although our indices directly measure the continental westerly flow near the surface rather than the upper-level jet, they are closely associated with strength, tilt and latitude of the Atlantic–European jet extension.The imprint of the indices in ERA5 sea-level pressure (SLP) and 500-hPa GPH (Fig. 1) follows the three base patterns (Extended Data Fig. 1). Increased blocking frequency24,25 over north-central Europe accompanies a poleward-shifted jet in winter. Analysing blocking in the ‘Twentieth Century reanalysis’ (20CRv3, 1806–2015, calculated for each member, then averaged)26 during extremes in the indices (below 2nd or above 98th percentile; Extended Data Fig. 2) shows even more pronounced patterns, suggesting an important role for weather variability and extreme weather.Correlations with temperature variability (based on anomalies from the mean seasonal cycle) are strong but change with season. In late winter, about half of the daily temperature variability in Denmark can be explained with the strength index (Padova minus Uppsala). This is the season when the continent is cold and the northeast–southwest temperature gradient is particularly strong (Extended Data Fig. 4). The tilt index shows the largest imprint in late spring (May), when the northern North Atlantic is cold, while the land has already warmed. Jet latitude has a large effect in summer (July) over Western Europe, when anticyclonic conditions establish (or not) over the continent. In fact, a combination of these three situations led to the coldest year in central Europe since 1421: 174027. In all, with only three indices based on four pressure series, a large fraction of daily temperature variability can be explained year-round—in some locations, up to 40% (Extended Data Fig. 4).The imprint of the indices in mean precipitation28 shows a relatively strong correlation over Western Europe. Unlike for temperature, there is hardly any seasonal difference.Drivers of extreme weatherClose relations to the jet indices are also found for extremes. We averaged indices (in this case standardized for comparability) on days with temperature, 24-h precipitation or wind speed28 above the 98th (below the 2nd) percentile per grid cell and plotted these averages as maps (Extended Data Fig. 5). Indices are typically outside ±2 standard deviations (roughly corresponding to the 2nd to 98th percentiles) for extreme wind speeds, ±1.5 for hot or cold days and ±1 for extreme precipitation in areas of a strong influence.We analysed extremes in the indices averaged over 1, 5 and 15 days. One-day events that are covered by 20CRv3 (Supplementary Table 3) are analysed for 2-m temperature, SLP, 500-hPa GPH, precipitation rate and 300-hPa wind (Fig. 2). Even though 20CRv3 has limitations in the early decades, consistent patterns of extreme weather are found. The day with the most positive strength occurred on 22 January 1993. The fields show blocking over south-western Europe and a strong pressure gradient over the North Sea. Severe storm surges hit northern Germany. The second strongest event in the 20CRv3 period was 16 February 1962, when a storm surge hit Hamburg causing the biggest natural disaster in Germany in the twentieth century. The day with the most negative strength, 26 December 1836, had strong easterly winds (>30 m s−1) at 300 hPa over England, embedded between two westerly jets at 70° N and 35° N, respectively, in a typical diffluent block situation. Heavy snowfall began in Southern England on 24 December and continued; snow drift formed. On 27 December 1836, an avalanche killed eight people in Lewes, East Sussex, the deadliest avalanche in history in the UK. Below freezing temperatures covered much of Spain.Fig. 2: Extreme jet index days.Full size imageFields of surface air temperature, 500-hPa GPH (contours, gpm) and 300-hPa wind (arrows) (first and third row) and precipitation rate and SLP (hPa) (second and fourth row) at 12 UTC on days with the most extreme indices (Supplementary Table 3). The light green contour shows 50% blocking frequency (averaged across the ensemble).The day with the most positive tilt index occurred on 5 February 1999. Strong north-westerly flow towards the Alps led to extensive snowfall, contributing to one of the worst avalanche winters in recent history in the Alps29. The most negative tilt, on 11 November 1891, shows strong south-westerly flow over Western Europe. The Portland Guardian (Friday, 13 November 1891, page 2) wrote: ‘A hurricane of fearful intensity is raging in the English Channel (…) [It] is the worst known for years’.The situation with the highest latitude index (23 January 1907) shows the jet at 70° N, while Central Europe was under the influence of easterly flow. In Sarajevo, daily mean temperature dropped to −18.5 °C, making it the fourth coldest day on record (1901–2025), while Northern Sweden experienced exceptionally high daily mean temperatures (+0.5 °C at Jokkmokk on the next day). Finally, on 26 February 1989, the jet at 300 hPa was over the Mediterranean. With an average temperature of 11 °C, this was the warmest February day on record at Lviv, Ukraine. In the Gulf of Biscay, hurricane-force winds sank the freighter Anna Leonhardt; 14 people died. The analysis shows that extremes in the jet indices lead to extreme weather over Europe. It also shows that the strongest cases shown in Fig. 2 are representative for extremes in the indices (Extended Data Fig. 2) and conversely extreme indices typically accompany the discussed surface weather extremes (Extended Data Fig. 5). The effect on daily weather extremes arguably proceeds through pronounced blocking patterns.Stratospheric and solar influencesOn a seasonal scale, the jet indices show imprints of volcanic eruptions and El Niño/Southern Oscillation, although internal variability dominates14. The daily resolution allows studying the imprint of short-term forcing effects such as sudden stratospheric warmings (SSWs) and solar storms. Major SSWs, defined as a collapse of the polar vortex in the upper stratosphere, can propagate downward by wave–mean flow interaction, eventually affecting the westerly circulation in the troposphere and extreme weather30. We analysed 55 major SSWs since 194031 (Supplementary Table 4), of which 33 are characterized as downward propagating, and composited the 15-day filtered jet indices around the dates of the major SSWs. Results agree with previous studies32 and show a weakening of the jet after 10–30 days, which corresponds to the expected downward propagation time (Fig. 3). We also find a significant equatorward shift with the same delay. Both effects are the strongest for downward propagating events (minor warmings show no effect; Methods).Fig. 3: Composites of 15-day averaged indices for SSWs or solar storms.Full size imageTop: composites for 55 major SSWs since 1940, of which 33 are characterized as downward propagating (prop.)31 (Supplementary Table 4), and 176 minor warming events. Bottom: composites for 102 solar or geomagnetic storms since 1730 that occurred in the September–March period (Supplementary Table 5) as well as for five subgroups (potential (pot.) EEPs comprise low-latitude aurorae, geomagnetic storms and fast transit events). Lines show the composite mean, and shading indicates the 95% confidence interval of the mean.We then composited strong solar storms back to 1730 on the basis of historical observations (Methods; Supplementary Table 5). Solar storms are often accompanied by increased solar energetic particle fluxes (including solar proton events (SPEs) and their extreme form, ground level enhancements (GLEs)) or by geomagnetic storms that trigger energetic electron precipitation (EEP) events. Both can generate HOx or NOx radicals in the polar mesosphere, typically at 60–80 km (energetic SPEs also further down), leading to ozone destruction both in the mesosphere and, through NOx transport, the stratosphere33,34,35. Associated differential atmospheric heating strengthens the stratospheric polar vortex36, potentially leading to a strengthened and poleward-shifted tropospheric jet37. A more rapid, subtropical link could also shift the jet poleward33. Owing to the higher altitude of the interaction, we expect a longer delay than for SSWs, presumably longer for EEP than SPEs. Sukhodolov et al.38 modelled the strongest known solar particle storm in 774/5 (assuming 1 September as the date of the storm) and found strengthened westerlies at the surface after 70 days. A review is given by Nesse et al.39.For compositing, we focused on the active season of stratosphere–troposphere coupling, that is, winter and early spring, but accounted for possibly longer downward propagation times and considered all 102 events between September, when the mesosphere–stratosphere Arctic polar vortex typically forms, and March.Results show a significant strengthening of the jet after 80–120 days (Fig. 3), which is robust when compositing subgroups (pre- and post-1940 events, potential EEPs, GLEs or other SPEs, each centred to the subgroup period mean for October–April); GLEs and SPEs also show earlier responses. Analyses of the strongest event per category (Extended Data Fig. 9) are consistent with these results. The jet is shifted poleward on average but not significantly. Our results show an impact of solar storms on the jet stream and thus a link between space weather and Earth’s weather.Changes over the last 300 yearsTo address long-term changes, we analysed the distribution of the daily jet indices by dividing the 300-year period into ten 30-year periods. Changes in the jet in the last 30-year period compared with earlier periods are analysed on the basis of the 2nd, 50th and 98th percentile. Clear changes are seen in the jet strength in the cold season (Fig. 4). The 2nd and 50th percentiles move upwards, pointing to a stronger jet with fewer negative extremes. The increase in the median since the pre-industrial period corresponds to 0.13 standard deviations of daily indices (1851–1950), and the increase of the 2nd percentile is even stronger (0.16 standard deviations). There were not more positive extremes in the last period compared with the previous 30-year period but more in the last 60 years compared with all earlier periods. The median of the tilt index decreased in both seasons (most clearly in the warm season), and the latitude index increased in the cold season. Positive extremes in the tilt index in the warm season decreased. Corresponding analyses for 5- and 15-day averages (Extended Data Fig. 6) show similar results. These changes are consistent with an observed strengthening of the jet reported in literature, although it should be noted that most literature analyses the upper-level jet, whereas our diagnostics describe the surface imprint.Fig. 4: Changes in the distribution of daily jet indices.Full size imageDensities of indices for the cold and warm season for ten 30-year periods between 1725 and 2024. Insets show 2nd, 50th and 98th percentiles (offset for visualization).Time series of seasonal means (Fig. 5; smoothed with a spline) confirm the increased cold-season strength, the strongly positive tilt in the eighteenth and early nineteenth century and an increasing cold-season latitude. The agreement of the indices with similarly filtered monthly indices18 at 500 hPa from ModE-RA (ensemble of 20)17 is good for cold-season jet strength but less good for other seasons and indices. Daily indices were also calculated from the ensemble of 20 atmospheric simulations underlying ModE-RA, that is, ModE-Sim40. Variations in common with ModE-RA indicate variability constrained by the model boundary conditions (for example, sea-surface temperatures, volcanic aerosols and greenhouse gases).Fig. 5: Development of the jet stream.Full size imageTime series of seasonal mean jet strength, tilt and latitude in different datasets (reconstruction, ModE-RA, ModE-Sim, CMIP6 historical and SSP2-4.5) smoothed with a spline fit. Insets with coloured dots show the means of the 2nd, 50th and 98th percentiles of the distribution, and filled orange symbols denote a significant difference between 1851–1880 and 2070–2100 across the different model simulations.Unlike for the 500-hPa indices, where all recent changes are within the variability of the past 600 years, the recent strength in the daily index in winter is outside the variability of the past 300 years and outside the ModE-Sim ensemble of the last 600 years. The same is true for the low values of tilt in the warm season. However, this comparison should be taken with care. Although all daily pressure series in observations and model simulations were standardized on the basis of the same period, the variability of the smoothed indices differs between datasets. This points to differences in the amplitude of variability at scales larger than daily. Strong excursions in the eighteenth century could point to remaining errors in the pressure measurements.Next, we compared the observation-based indices to indices derived from the historical simulations from the Climate Model Intercomparison Project (CMIP6)41 (Supplementary Table 6). Their smoothed time series exhibit a higher variability than ModE-Sim, mostly encompassing the observations. The observed recent jet strengthening is at the upper edge of the distribution of CMIP6 historical but outside of the distribution of ModE-Sim. The distributions (right insets) show that ModE-Sim and CMIP6 historical both underestimate the 98th percentile for strength and tilt in both seasons, but both overestimate the 98th percentile for jet latitude in the cold season.Future changes in jet stream indicesTo assess future changes in the jet, we analysed the SSP2-4.5 scenario (results for the SSP3-7.0 and SSP5-8.5 scenarios are shown in Extended Data Figs. 7 and 8, respectively) and compared the two 30-year periods 1851–1880 and 2071–2100. The jet will get stronger in the cold season and more tilted in the warm season, whereas the other indices and seasons show no significant trends. However, we find increasing trends in the 2nd percentile and decreasing trends in the 98th percentile in all seasons and indices; many of them (including all six trends of the 2nd percentile) are significant. This indicates that the jet gets less extreme. This result is the same for all scenarios; in the stronger scenarios, the magnitudes of the trends are stronger and we additionally find a poleward shift of the median in the cold season. However, CMIP6 models have been shown to exhibit inconsistencies, which therefore need to be interpreted with care.The projected strengthening of the cold-season jet is in line with the observed changes in the recent decades4,5,6,7,8,9. However, it is not seen in the warm season and it is not seen in extremes. The upper-level jet depends on the temperature gradient near the tropopause, which increases as the tropical upper troposphere warms and the Arctic lower stratosphere cools and might explain the increased strength12. This is however not the case for the surface, where temperature gradients decrease. The vertical structure of the trend as well as the consistent decrease in extremes across all indices and seasons in the CMIP6 scenario simulations (and partly in the observations) therefore requires further investigation.MethodsUppsala, Padova and London pressure seriesThe Uppsala daily pressure series was taken from the IMPROVE project22 from 1722 to 2000 and from Uppsala University (SMHI) from January 2001 to September 2023. For gap filling and for comparison, we consulted a series from Stockholm, 1756–2012, from the IMPROVE project42. We found sometimes large differences of up to 30 hPa or more despite the spatial proximity. We analysed all differences larger than 10 hPa in comparison with the days before and after and with neighbouring stations. This led to flagging and removing 565 values in the Uppsala series and 32 in the Stockholm series.The Padova daily pressure series was taken from the IMPROVE project21 and covers 1725–1997. For homogenization, we applied the published correction amounts and techniques21. We used station data from Rovereto (1782–1849) and Milan (1763–1862)43 to fill gaps in the next step. The data from December 1997 to December 2009 were taken from Treviso (ISPD) and from January 2010 to September 2023 from Teolo (ARPAV).The London daily pressure series was based on homogenized subdaily data19, covering 1691–2023. The data were averaged to daily means and then merged by file number.Berlin pressure seriesThe daily Berlin pressure series consists of data from several segments presented in Supplementary Table 1. The longest historical segments are those from the Kirch family, 1721–177444, and Brand, 1760–1794, whereas the data from the German weather service (DWD) start only in 1876. Earlier gaps and gaps between the Brand series and the DWD series were filled with series from Jablonski, 1725–1727; Lambert, 1769–1777; and Gronau, 1775–1801, from Berlin as well as several other series from nearby cities, including Loebau, 1720–1730; Wittenberg, 1728–1729; Žitenice, 1807–1818; and Jena, 1824–1990. The 6-year gap between Žitenice and Jena was filled with data from 20CRv3. Because of an obvious drop in the variance in this period owing to the fact that the ensemble mean is too smooth, we inflated the variance in 20CRv3 by removing the seasonal cycle, multiplying the residual with the ratio of the standard deviations of the observations and 20CRv3 and adding back the seasonal cycle.Auxiliary pressure seriesThe following auxiliary pressure series were used to fill gaps in the data series. This was most relevant in the eighteenth century, when gaps were the most frequent. We used a series from De Bilt, 1743 to present19, which we back-extended to 1738 (Zwanenburg), and a daily pressure series from Paris20. Further, two series from Nuremberg were used27, covering 1722–1743. From Switzerland, we used the series from Zurich (1718–1733) and Neuchâtel (1753–1782)45. A series from Montpellier (1706–1748) was also used. However, this series is clearly of lower quality and consists to a considerable extent of extrema, that is, we have typically approximately six values per month, which always include the lowest and highest pressure. For testing and homogenizing this dataset, we first used the analogue-resampling and off-line Ensemble Kalman Filter technique described below to generate a daily reference series. We found a correlation of this reference series with the (independent) observations of 0.55 on the basis of deseasonalized data. Then, we used this reference for breakpoint detection and homogenization (see below).Pre-processing and testingIn the first step, all series were averaged to daily means (if subdaily). We then performed a sequence of outlier tests, marking measurements (1) outside the interval 950–1060 hPa, (2) outside the interval −5/+4 standard deviations (as negative extremes are more common), (3) steps of 30 hPa or more in a day and (4) four or more consecutive identical values. All 2,761 marked measurements were analysed individually by analysing two or more time steps before and after and by analysing all available stations. Most of the marked measurements were kept, as they were well in line with the other stations. Only about 5% were eventually flagged.After this procedure, Craddock and Pettitt tests were performed on all series. The former is a graphical test46 based on the cumulative sum of differences to a reference series, whose shape indicates the type (step or trend) of an inhomogeneity as well as the breakpoints; the latter is a non-parametric test for breakpoints47. The series of Uppsala, Padova and London had already been homogenized by other authors and tests confirmed their homogeneity. The Berlin series was homogenized (that is, adjusted for breaks) by using several reference series from DWD after 1876 and from the HCLIM48 dataset before that. Each segment in Supplementary Table 1 was first homogenized independently and then merged with the others by proceeding backward in time and adjusting the older segment according to the overlap with the more recent one (in one case, the Prague series from HCLIM was used as reference instead because the overlap was too short). The list of corrected breakpoints (detected using the Craddock test with the support of some metadata such as station relocations or instrument changes) is presented in Supplementary Table 7. The corrections were calculated for each calendar month as the medians across all reference series and then smoothed to the calendar days by fitting the first two harmonics of a Fourier series to avoid jumps between months. In two cases, large breakpoints were separated by only a few months (in 1760/61 in the Kirch series and 1794 in the Gronau series), leaving insufficient data for a reliable correction; the data between those breakpoints were considered invalid and removed.Furthermore, also some of the auxiliary series were found to be inhomogeneous and were homogenized. Neuchâtel was corrected by −3.06 hPa before 1/1765. Afterwards, the entire series was detrended (adding −0.58 hPa yr−1), as the Craddock test revealed a trend inhomogeneity. The Zurich series was corrected by −4.87 hPa before 1/1729. For both Neuchâtel and Zurich, we used the London series to determine the correction, but the inhomogeneities were also found when using Padova, Paris, Uppsala or De Bilt as reference. After homogenization, the two series were standardized separately and then merged. The Montpellier series showed a likely inhomogeneity on 1 May 1741, which we corrected on the basis of the generated reference series.For the further procedure, all series were deseasonalized and standardized (DS) by subtracting the first two harmonics of the seasonal cycle and dividing the residuals by the standard deviation on the basis of the entire available respective time period. This means that the series of Zwanenburg and De Bilt were standardized individually, as were the two series from Nuremberg. Therefore, no homogenization is required in these cases.Gap fillingThe further processing was based on DS data because the index series will later be defined on the basis of DS data and because there might be biases in the mean, in the seasonal cycle (through a temperature dependence) and in the variability (owing to the number of measurements per day). First, we filled gaps by means of neighbouring stations (Stockholm for Uppsala, Rovereto or Milan for Padova) on the basis of DS data and then back-converted them to absolute values using the coefficients and standard deviations of Padova and Uppsala, respectively (Supplementary Table 8). Then we proceeded similarly and filled remaining gaps with DS reanalysis data from the closest grid cell at 12 UTC. From here onwards, we used 1851–1950 as a base period for standardization (1940–1989 for ERA5). Gaps were filled (also in the auxiliary series) with data from ERA5 if the gap was between 1940 and 2024, or from 20CRv3 if it was earlier. After this procedure, a small fraction of gaps remained (Supplementary Table 8). For filling these gaps, we used an analogue method augmented with an off-line Ensemble Kalman Filter approach49. On the basis of all series (including DS auxiliary series), we searched for the best analogue in the 1940–2024 period using the Euclidean distance. The best analogue was further augmented using an off-line Ensemble Kalman Filter, with covariances specified from the best 200 analogues. The observation error covariance R was set to 0.16, which corresponds to an observation error of approximately 4 hPa (the same approach was used for generating a reference dataset for the Montpellier pressure series). To estimate the skill of the in-filling, we evaluated the procedure in the year 1868, alternatingly reconstructing each series from its neighbours. We found relatively high correlations (Supplementary Table 8), except for Uppsala (r = 0.56), which (after merging with Stockholm, 20CRv3 and ERA5) had only two missing days in the past 300 years. Note that the gap filling only concerns a few values (most of them in the Berlin series), mostly in the 1720s to 1750s as well as some in the 1760s and 1770s. The two homogenized series from Paris and De Bilt contribute the most to filling gaps, followed by the series from Neuchâtel (each contributes to fill more than 1,000 gaps). The two series from Nuremberg and Zurich contribute very little (each less than 90 filled gaps), as they do not overlap with periods in which many gaps were observed.We provide the pressure series in different formats, including the quality-controlled, homogenized data and their quality flags (for all series, including the auxiliary series), the gap-filled standardized data and the gap-filled data converted back to pressure using the standard deviations and coefficients of the four series.Climate modelsWe selected all CMIP6 models that provide SLP and that have no missing years. We selected the historical runs and the scenarios SSP2-4.5, SSP3-7.0 and SSP5-8.5. For each scenario, we only used models that have both the historical run and the corresponding scenario run, and only one run was selected per model. The models and simulations are presented in Supplementary Table 6. Likewise, we used all 20 ensemble members from ModE-Sim (sets 1420-3 and 1850-1).In each simulation, we extracted the grid points closest to the locations of Padova, Uppsala, London and Berlin. For forming the indices, we subtracted the first two harmonics of the seasonal cycle and divided the residuals by the standard deviation (both derived from the 1851–1950 period). Significance between the periods across the model simulations was calculated with a Wilcoxon rank sum test (which is equivalent to the Mann–Whitney test).IndicesThe indices are defined in a similar way as other pressure indices (for example, the North Atlantic Oscillation (NAO) index) as differences between (or sums of) standardized, deseasonalized pressure series:Strength = PPadova – PUppsalaTilt = PLondon – 0.33 × (PBerlin + PPadova + PUppsala)Latitude = 0.33 × (PLondon + PBerlin) + 0.1667 × (PPadova + PUppsala).All indices were standardized on the basis of the 1851–1950 period (except in ERA5, where we used 1940–1989). The three indices are largely uncorrelated (correlation coefficients over all seasons and years are 0.13 for strength and tilt as well as for tilt and latitude and 0.07 for strength and latitude). Correlations with a daily NAO index from 1836 to 201550 in the cold season are 0.393, 0.175 and 0.142 for strength, tilt and latitude indices. This indicates that our indices are related to but different from the classical NAO, arguably owing to the different longitude (Uppsala is 17.5° E in the jet extension region, Reykjavik is 22° W in the core region of the jet).To address longer timescales, we used a moving average of 5 and 15 days, respectively. Averaging the daily indices to monthly means and then comparing them with the indices derived from monthly ERA5 500-hPa GPH fields yields high correlations (approximately 0.75) for strength and tilt in both seasons but lower (approximately 0.62) for jet latitude. There is no one-to-one relation to monthly indices of the NAO, the East Atlantic Pattern (EA) and the Scandinavian pattern (SCAND) of the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) Climate Prediction Centre51. The jet strength is weakly (0.31) correlated with the NAO and more strongly (−0.51) with SCAND, tilt is negatively correlated with both NAO (−0.44) and EA (−0.45), whereas latitude is weakly (0.28) correlated with EA.We also compared the indices with independent monthly frequencies of wind direction over the English Channel52 back to 1685 (Supplementary Table 2) and found positive (negative) correlations of the jet strength index with the fraction of days per month with westerly (northerly and easterly) wind. Jet tilt is positively (negatively) correlated with the fraction of northerly (southerly) winds, while jet latitude is positively (negatively) correlated with the fraction of easterly (westerly) wind. Correlations are not very strong (±0.3–0.4) but consistent over time and season.The three series are stationary over time. Two-year moving time series of lag-1 autocorrelation and of the variance do not reveal obvious changes (Extended Data Fig. 3). The autocorrelation for the tilt index is higher in the station-based indices than in ERA5, but this also the case for all model simulations. A lower quality of pressure measurements is expected in the early decades when instruments were poorer, procedures were not standardized, fewer redundant information was available for quality control and there were no good reference series for homogenization.To confirm that the indices explain day-to-day temperature variability also in the past, we used long daily temperature series from 14 sites for 1765–1864, a period with good data coverage and calculated anomalies from the mean seasonal cycle based on this period: Bologna53, Padova54, Milan43, Cadiz55, Berlin56, the Central England temperature57, the Swiss Plateau temperature series58, Geneva and Basel59, Paris60, Uppsala22, Stockholm42, St. Petersburg61 and Haarlem (KNMI). Correlations (Fig. 1, circles) confirm the results from ERA5.To analyse low-frequency variability, we formed seasonal averages and then smoothed these with a spline with a smoothing parameter of 0.57 or a locally estimated scatterplot smoothing regression with a window size of 42 years, both of which give almost undistinguishable results and correspond approximately to a 30-year moving average. We show the spline results in this paper.Stratospheric warmings and solar stormsTo composite SSWs, we used a list of major warmings (defined as a reversal of the zonal mean zonal wind at 10 hPa at 60° N in ERA5) from Lu et al.31 based on ERA5, which we complemented backward to January 1940 and forward to December 2024 by adding three events (Supplementary Table 4). We also composited 176 minor warmings (defined as the first day of a minimum 5-day reversal of the temperature gradient at 10 hPa between 60° N and the North Pole in ERA5 that is not accompanied by a wind reversal). The results (Fig. 3) show no signal, as expected.Lists of historical solar storms that could be used for compositing are not readily available. Several authors provide lists from different types of solar storms, which we combined (Supplementary Table 5). Evidence comes from reported low-latitude aurorae (back to the eighteenth century), geomagnetic storms (nineteenth century) or fast interplanetary shock events (fast-transit events, nineteenth century), all of which indicate potential EEP events. GLEs and SPEs were observed after the 1940s (neutron monitors) and after 1976 (satellites), respectively. In total, we used 102 storms in September–March (Supplementary Table 5). Note that near solar maximum years, storms often occur in short intervals. Although we require a 15-day distance between events, storm effects may overlap in the displayed 130-day time interval and smooth the signal. We also composited pre-1940 storms (n = 28), post-1940 storms (n = 74), potential EEP events (geomagnetic storms, low-latitude aurorae and fast-transit events, n = 67), GLEs (n = 30) and strong SPEs that are not GLEs (>1,000 proton flux units, n = 13).

AbstractAmazonia is highly sensitive to climate extremes, yet we lack an Amazon-wide assessment that examines the spatial-temporal changes in these extreme conditions. We address this within seasons and across the hydrological year, using a quantiles approach that integrates the frequency and magnitude of climate extremes and by linking changes in temperature with evapotranspiration. We show that high temperature extremes and temperature-linked measures of water deficit are both changing at a much faster rate than central trends. The 95th percentile of maximum temperatures in the driest period increased by 0.49 °C per decade (dec-1) compared to 0.21°C dec-1 for the central trend of mean temperatures for the year. Crucially, over 700,000 square kilometres in central-north Amazonia have experienced increases in extreme dry season temperatures ≥ 0.75 °C dec-1 ( ≥ 3.22 °C over 43 years). Adaptation measures for these rapid changes in climate extremes must include preventing the deforestation and disturbances that amplify risks.

                            Tropical ecology

IntroductionThe frequency and intensity of climate extremes have increased in many regions of the world1 and are predicted to increase further under future climate change scenarios2. These extremes are responsible for some of the greatest climate-linked impacts on nature and people, driving increases in human morbidity and mortality3,4, losses of forest species5 and ecosystem degradation6. Climate extremes are also responsible for deleterious changes in some of the world’s most important ecosystems. In Amazonia, recent exceptionally hot or dry periods have led to extensive and unprecedented forest fires7,8,9, large-scale tree mortality10, and localised animal mortality11, extreme warming of waters12, and negative outcomes for human access to services13 and health14,15,16. An increase in the incidence and severity of climate extremes could therefore help push Amazonia past critical thresholds, leading to much larger-scale deterioration of social and ecological conditions17,18,19.Given the importance of climate extremes in Amazonia, it is crucial to understand the temporal and spatial distribution of change. Although the central trends of temperature change in Amazonia are tracking global averages20,21,22, these are often poor predictors of the trends of climate extremes1. This is particularly the case in South America, where the divergences between changes in mean and extreme temperatures are widespread, but variable1. Inferences from global, pantropical or regional studies on changes in climate extremes are currently insufficient. Many report only annual averages, which are known to mask ecologically important seasonal changes23. Others simplify the substantial spatial and temporal heterogeneity in dry season length and onset that exists across Amazonia24 (Supplementary Fig. 1) by defining dry season timing according to the drier period in the southern Amazon20,25,26 or across large sub-regions21,22,27. In addition, most focus on changes in either temperature, precipitation or water deficit, and therefore fall short of the integrated approach required to understand drivers of key ecological responses such as vegetation productivity and mortality28 and forest flammability29.Here, we provide a comprehensive assessment of the changing central (50th percentile) and extreme trends (5th and 95th percentiles) of multiple climate variables across the 7 million km2 region of Amazonia (see Methods), based on 11 km spatial resolution (57,900 grid cells) from 1981 to 2023 (43 years). Our analysis of extreme trends is not intended to identify particular extreme events as others have done8,10,30, but instead, focuses on the trends in the tails of conditional distributions (climate variables over time). This approach provides an integrated way to understand the changes in both the frequency and the intensity of extreme events across the whole time series.To do this, we first divide the year into 73 pentads to explore changes across hydrological years, following approaches used to identify changes in dry season timing across extensive subregions22,31. However, we extend this so that each grid square has its own hydrological periodicity, with annual or seasonal periods starting with the wettest pentad or month instead of calendar years or fixed months (Supplementary Fig. 2). This allowed us to assess daily averages of minimum, mean and maximum temperature and Vapour Pressure Deficit (VPD) during the driest period as well as across the hydrological year. For rainfall, we evaluated the driest and wettest periods and the intensification of the water cycle through changes in rainfall amplitude. We also integrate changes in temperature with changes in rainfall or humidity, analysing variation in VPD and Maximum Cumulative Water Deficit (MCWD) that are well-established predictors of both plant physiology and fire activity30,32. MCWD was calculated in two ways: using a fixed 100 mm of evapotranspiration per month commonly used in the literature30,33 (MCWD100) and by allowing evapotranspiration to increase with temperature (MCWDTemp) following modelled estimates of temperature and atmospheric CO2 responses34 that are broadly supported by recent observations35. Finally, we identified the metrics and regions showing the greatest rates of change and also assessed whether higher rates of change are associated with historically warmer or drier conditions.We show that Amazonia’s climate has changed rapidly, but not uniformly. Extremes are changing at a much higher rate than central trends, and Amazonia-wide shifts in temperature—rather than precipitation—are driving most of the changes in water deficit and VPD. Crucially, we identified a hitherto under-emphasised and spatially distinct region of high climate change in the central-north Amazon. We discuss these results considering their implications for climate adaptation, conservation and sustainability in Amazonia.Results and discussionClimate change across AmazoniaOn average, the rate of change of extreme temperatures from 1981 to 2023 was faster than the central trend (Fig. 1, Supplementary Fig. 3). For central trends, annual mean temperatures increased by a mean rate of 0.21 °C per decade (dec-1), (Interquartile Range IQR: 0.15 °C–0.27 °C dec-1) and 0.90 °C between 1981 and 2023, which is in line with the global average and previous estimates for Amazonia20 (Fig. 1a). However, the 95th percentile of mean temperatures increased at a mean rate of at least 0.30 °C dec-1 (IQR:0.24 °C–0.36 °C dec-1) and 1.29 °C over 43 years (Fig. 1a). As expected, the rate of increase was greater in the driest period than across the whole hydrological year21, with maximum temperature at the 95th percentile increasing by 0.49 °C dec-1 (IQR: 0.35 °C–0.63 °C dec-1) (Fig. 1a). This corresponds to an increase of 2.11 °C over 43 years, 2.34 times higher than the annual mean central trend (Fig. 1a).Fig. 1: The magnitude of climate change across the Amazon region over 43 years (1981-2023).Full size imageDecadal rates of change of (a) temperature (°C per decade) (b) vapour-pressure deficit (VPD; kPa per decade) and (c) maximum cumulative water deficit (MCWD; mm per decade). All panels show the rate of change for the central trend (50th percentile) and extreme (95th percentile for temperature and VPD; 5th percentile for MCWD), calculated on grid cell-wise with a spatial resolution of 11 km. Trends for minimum, mean and maximum temperature and mean VPD were calculated for the hydrological year (Year) and driest period (DP) considering pentad means (5-day period). MCWD was calculated considering two evapotranspiration (ET) thresholds, one fixed at 100 mm and the other linked to temperature. In all panels, coloured dots represent the Amazon-wide mean rate of change per decade for each variable in each period for the central (yellow) and extreme (red) trends. Black dashed vertical lines correspond to zero. The panel for all variables is available in Supplementary Fig. 3.Temperature-linked measures of maximum cumulative water deficit (MCWDTemp) and the vapour pressure deficit (VPD) also showed large changes over time, with higher values for extreme percentiles. For VPD, increases in the 95th percentiles were about one-third higher than for the central trend, for both annual and driest periods (Fig. 1b). VPD also had the greatest rate of change during the driest period, increasing by 0.06 kPa dec-1 at the central trend (IQR: 0.02-0.09 kPa dec-1) and 0.26 kPa over 43 years. This was even higher at the 95th percentile, increasing by 0.08 kPa dec-1 (IQR :0.04–0.12 kPa dec-1; 0.34 kPa over 43 years) (Fig. 1b). For MCWD, which is scaled towards the negative, the 5th percentile represents the drier extreme. The mean rate of change at the 5th percentile of MCWDTemp was −12.75 mm dec-1 (IQR: −22.88 to −0.96 mm dec-1) and −54.82 mm over 43 years. This was twice that of the central trend of MCWDTemp of −6.61 mm dec-1 and −28.42 mm over 43 years (Fig. 1c). The temperature-invariant measure of MCWD100 showed no directional trend, with the 50th percentile changing by just 0.03 mm dec-1 (IQR: −5.13 to 4.01 mm dec-1) and 0.13 mm over 43 years ( Fig. 1c).Precipitation increased across the central, 5th and 95th percentiles for both annual and wettest periods of the year, but the trends were close to zero when assessing only the driest period (Supplementary Fig. 3d). For the central trend, annual precipitation increased by a mean rate of 31.29 mm dec-1 (IQR: −8.14 to 65.28 mm dec-1) and 134.55 mm over 43 years; Supplementary Fig. 3d). Precipitation amplitude showed a slight increase at all percentiles, with the greatest at the 95th percentile, where intensification of the water cycle—the difference between the wettest and driest periods—rose by a mean rate of 14.95 mm dec-1 (IQR: −19.29 to 51.42 mm dec-1) or 64.28 mm over 43 years (Supplementary Fig. 3e).Spatial variation and hotspots of climate changeAmazonia-wide averages encompass considerable regional variation, with pronounced spatial divergence among the regions most affected by the highest rates of change at the 50th and extreme percentiles (Fig. 2, Supplementary Figs. 4–8). For the central trend of change across the hydrological year, our results are broadly consistent with previous work, and the southern Amazon stands out as the region most affected by increases in temperature and temperature-linked variables such as VPD (Fig. 2 and Supplementary Figs. 4, 5)21,36. However, at the 95th percentile, the greatest rates of change for temperature and VPD are concentrated in a central-northern region (Fig. 2a, b) that has rarely been identified as being imperilled by climate change. Here, changes in average maximum temperature and mean VPD in the driest period were particularly alarming, with 10% of the biome surpassing rates of increase of 0.75 °C dec-1 ( > 3.22 °C over 43 years) and 0.14 kPa dec-1 ( > 0.60 kPa over 43 years). The region was also a locus of change in MCWDtemp, with extreme years seeing rates of change of −35.02 mm dec-1 (< −150.59 mm over 43 years) (Fig. 2).Fig. 2: Spatial distribution of climate change across the Amazon over 43 years (1981–2023).Full size imageDecadal rates of change were calculated grid cell-wise at 11 km spatial resolution for (a) the mean and maximum temperature (b) mean vapour-pressure deficit (VPD) and (c) maximum cumulative water deficit (MCWD). The rates of change for temperature (°C per decade) and VPD (kPa per decade) are shown, along with both the central (50th) and upper extreme (95th percentile) trends, for the hydrological year (Year) and the driest period (DP). For MCWD, the rate of change is shown for the central trend (50th percentile) and the lower extreme (5th percentile) considering a temperature-linked evapotranspiration threshold. Maps for all variables, percentiles and periods are available in Supplementary Figs. 4–8.There was a strong spatial signal to the difference between central and extreme rates of climate change (Fig. 3). In much of the southern and southeastern Amazon, central trends are growing at a similar rate to—or even slightly faster than—the 95th percentile of temperature and VPD or 5th percentile of MCWDtemp. In contrast, in the central-north region the rate of change of climate extremes (95th percentiles for temperature and VPD, 5th percentiles for MCWDtemp) diverged greatly from both the central trends and the opposite extremes (Fig. 3a). Overlaying the top deciles of rates of change at the central and most extreme trends (95th percentile for mean temperature in the hydrological year, maximum temperature and VPD in the driest period of the hydrological year with the 5th percentile for MCWDTemp) highlights critical regions where the fastest rates of change are co-occuring (Fig. 4). For central trends, there was strong spatial agreement between temperature and VPD, while MCWDTemp was also prevalent on the southern borders of Amazonia. For the extreme trends, temperature-VPD overlaps were also extensive, but critical areas for MCWDTemp included additional regions at the periphery of Amazonia (Fig. 4).
